title: Logarithms and Logarithmic Functions

confusionCorner.body: The argument $y$ in $\log_b y$ must be [[imp:positive]]. You cannot take the log of zero or a negative number. That's because no real exponent can make a positive base $b$ equal zero or a negative number.
confusionCorner.title: Argument Must Be Positive

explanation: A [[kw:logarithm]] is the inverse operation to exponentiation. The statement $\log_b y = x$ means $b^x = y$.
$b$ is the [[kw:base]] of the logarithm, $y$ is the argument (must be positive), and $x$ is the exponent.
The equations $\log_b y = x$ (logarithmic form) and $b^x = y$ (exponential form) are equivalent.
Two special values: $\log_b 1 = 0$ (since $b^0 = 1$) and $\log_b b = 1$ (since $b^1 = b$).
A [[kw:common logarithm]] is base 10, written $\log_{10} x$ or simply $\log x$. A [[kw:natural logarithm]] is base $e$, written $\ln x$.

teacherCues: Write $2^x = 8$ and ask: What is $x$? Then write $2^x = 6$ and ask: How can we express $x$?
Introduce the definition: $\log_b y = x$ if and only if $b^x = y$. Show that logarithms are exponents.

explanation: To evaluate a logarithm $\log_b y$ by hand, ask: $b$ raised to what power equals $y$? That power is the answer.
A [[kw:common logarithm]] ($\log$) has base 10. A [[kw:natural logarithm]] ($\ln$) has base $e$.
Use the LOG and LN keys on a calculator for bases other than 10 and $e$. For other bases, use the change‑of‑base formula (later) or guess‑and‑check with powers.

blocks.title: Inverse Properties of Logarithms

hints: Log base 2 and base 2 exponent cancel.
The base $e$ and natural log cancel.

questions.prompt: What is the inverse of $f(x) = \log_5 x$? (Use f^(-1)(x) = ... format)
hints: The inverse of a logarithmic function is exponential.

explanation: The logarithmic function $g(x) = \log_b x$ is the [[kw:inverse]] of the exponential function $f(x) = b^x$.
Two inverse properties: $\log_b b^x = x$ (for any real $x$) and $b^{\log_b x} = x$ (for $x > 0$).
For common logs: $\log 10^x = x$, $10^{\log x} = x$.
For natural logs: $\ln e^x = x$, $e^{\ln x} = x$.
To find the inverse of a logarithmic function, switch $x$ and $y$ and write in exponential form.

confusionCorner.title: Domain of the Inverse
confusionCorner.body: When finding the inverse of a logarithmic function, remember that the original function's domain ($x >$ something) becomes the range of the inverse. The inverse's domain will be all real numbers for exponential functions.

discoveryHook.scenario: Because logs and exponentials are inverses, they cancel each other out—just like addition and subtraction. $10^{\log 4}$ simplifies instantly to 4, and $\ln e^{5} = 5$. This is the key to solving exponential equations.

explanation: Because $f(x) = \log_b x$ is the inverse of $g(x) = b^x$, the graph of $f$ is the reflection of $g$ across the line $y = x$.
For $b > 1$, the graph of $\log_b x$ passes through $(1,0)$, increases slowly, and has a [[kw:vertical asymptote]] at $x = 0$ (the $y$-axis).
Domain: $x > 0$. Range: all real numbers.
For $0 < b < 1$, the graph also passes through $(1,0)$ but decreases from left to right.
Transformations (shifts, stretches) apply to logarithmic graphs just like other functions.

formulaCard.formula: $$ f(x) = \log_b x $$ $$ \text{Domain: } x > 0, \text{ Range: all reals, Vertical Asymptote: } x = 0 $$

confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Domain
confusionCorner.body: Always check that the argument of the logarithm is positive. A solution that makes the argument $\le 0$ is [[imp:extraneous]] and must be rejected.

rows.1: Convert to exponential form; solve; use inverse properties if needed.
Check solution(s) in original equation; discard extraneous.

explanation: [[imp:Understand]]: Identify the logarithmic form. Note the base, argument, and what the logarithm equals. Check domain restrictions (argument must be $> 0$).
[[imp:Solve]]: Rewrite the equation in exponential form using the definition. Solve the resulting equation. If there are multiple logs, use inverse properties to simplify.
[[imp:Conclude]]: State the solution and verify it satisfies the original logarithmic equation. Discard any solutions that make the argument non‑positive.

steps: Understand: Base = 2, argument = $x+1$, value = 3. Domain: $x+1 > 0 \Rightarrow x > -1$.
Solve: Convert to exponential form: $2^3 = x+1$ → $8 = x+1$ → $x = 7$.

presenterNotes: Emphasize that a logarithm is an exponent. This is the single most important concept for students to grasp.
When converting between forms, use arrows to show the base stays the same, the exponent becomes the output, and the result becomes the argument.
For evaluating logs, start with simple powers of the base. Then move to fractional and negative exponents.
The inverse relationship is key to solving equations. Spend time on simplifying expressions like $\log_b b^x$ and $b^{\log_b x}$.
Graphing log functions by reflecting the exponential graph helps students visualize the asymptote and domain.
In the Blueprint block, emphasize checking the domain. Extraneous solutions can appear when solving log equations.
